prompt: In cache-aside, what does the application do on a miss?
hint: The `dashboard()` function.

choices.text: Asks the database, stores the answer with a TTL, returns it
choices.why: Right: the cache is filled only with answers somebody asked for.

choices.text: Returns an empty dashboard
choices.why: Nothing in cache-aside fills keys in the background; the reader does it.

choices.text: Waits for Redis to fetch the rows from PostgreSQL
choices.why: Redis never talks to PostgreSQL; the application talks to both.

choices.text: Raises an error
choices.why: A miss is the normal path, 200 times in the benchmark.

prompt: Of the 5000 dashboard requests through the cache, how many reached the database?
hint: The misses.

prompt: Why does `dashboard.py` cast the sum with `::bigint`?
hint: What type does PostgreSQL give a sum of integers, and can JSON hold it in Python?

choices.text: To make the query use the index on `seller_id`
choices.why: A cast in the select list does not change which index is used.

choices.text: Because the sum would overflow a 32-bit integer for big sellers
choices.why: sum of integers is already bigint-safe as numeric; the issue is the Python type.

choices.text: So the sum arrives as an int, not a Decimal
choices.why: Right: sum of integers is numeric, which psycopg returns as Decimal.

choices.text: Redis only accepts 64-bit numbers
choices.why: The value is stored as a JSON string; Redis does not look inside.

prompt: A search page caches each result under the exact text typed, `search:<text>`. The hit rate stays near 3%. What does the lesson's list say is wrong?
hint: Who asks the same question twice?

choices.text: The TTL is too long
choices.why: A longer TTL would raise the hit rate, not lower it.

choices.text: Redis is out of memory and evicting keys
choices.why: Possible in principle, but the lesson's point is that the questions rarely repeat.

choices.text: The searches should use a materialized view instead, refreshed every night
choices.why: A view per arbitrary search text has the same problem and worse.

choices.text: Few people type the same text, so most keys are never read again
choices.why: Right: a cache pays only for the same question asked by many.

prompt: After the order for seller 7 committed, `python3 dashboard.py 7` still said 91 orders. Why?
hint: Where did the answer come from?

choices.text: The INSERT had not committed yet
choices.why: psql -c commits; the database already said 92.

choices.text: It came from the cache, stored before the order
choices.why: Right: cache-aside serves the stored answer until the TTL ends.

choices.text: The dashboard only counts delivered orders, not pending ones
choices.why: The query counts every status; after the TTL it said 92.

choices.text: Redis rounds counts down to save memory
choices.why: Redis stores exactly the JSON it was given.

prompt: With a 60-second TTL and no invalidation, for how long is a change invisible on average, by the section's reasoning?
hint: Worst case the whole TTL, best case nothing.

choices.text: Sixty seconds, every time
choices.why: Only a change right after a store waits the whole TTL.

choices.text: Never, since Redis notices the change
choices.why: Redis never sees the database; nothing notices.

choices.text: About thirty seconds
choices.why: Right: half the TTL on average, the whole of it at worst.

choices.text: Two minutes, because the TTL restarts on every read
choices.why: `cache.get` does not reset a TTL; only `set` does.

prompt: Why does the lesson keep a TTL even when every write invalidates its keys?
hint: What happens if a delete is lost?

choices.text: Redis refuses to store a key that has no TTL once its memory is full
choices.why: Redis accepts keys with no expiry at all.

choices.text: It bounds how long a value survives when an invalidation is lost
choices.why: Right: a crash between commit and delete, or a forgotten key, is then wrong for a minute rather than for good.

choices.text: Without a TTL the hit rate drops to zero
choices.why: Without a TTL the hit rate rises; staleness is the problem.

choices.text: A TTL makes the dashboard query cheaper, since fewer rows are cached
choices.why: The query costs the same; the TTL only decides when it runs again.

prompt: Match each cached value with the TTL the section's table gives it.
hint: How stale can each screen be?

pairs.right: an hour, with invalidation on edit
a few seconds, or no cache

prompt: Put the steps of the race in `race.py` in the order that leaves a stale value in the cache.
hint: The delete happens before the stale store.
items: A misses the cache and reads the database
trap: If A stores before B deletes, the delete removes the stale value and nothing goes wrong.

prompt: In the unguarded run, what did reader C see?
hint: The last line of the first run.

choices.text: The cache empty, because B deleted the key
choices.why: A stored its value after the delete, so the key was there again.

choices.text: An error from Redis
choices.why: Nothing failed; that is what makes the race dangerous.

choices.text: 93 in the cache and 93 in the database
choices.why: The cache held A's older read.

choices.text: 92 cached, 93 in the database
choices.why: Right: the value read before the write was stored after the delete.

prompt: In the guarded run, what made reader A not store its value?
hint: The writer changes one more key.

choices.text: The version it noted had changed by store time
choices.why: Right: WATCH and MULTI/EXEC make the store conditional on that version.

choices.text: The TTL had already expired by the time it came to store
choices.why: Nothing was stored yet, so no TTL was running.

choices.text: PostgreSQL locked the order row until the writer committed
choices.why: The guard is entirely in Redis.

choices.text: B held a lock in Redis
choices.why: There is no lock here; the guard is a version compared at store time.

prompt: A team adds a nightly bulk import that updates thousands of orders directly in SQL. Their dashboards use cache-aside with delete-on-write in the web code and a 24-hour TTL. What does the section predict?
hint: Who has to invalidate?

choices.text: The import's changes appear within a minute, as the TTL rolls over
choices.why: Only if something deletes the keys; the TTL here is a day.

choices.text: Redis notices the UPDATE and drops the keys
choices.why: Redis never sees the database.

choices.text: Screens keep the old figures for up to a day
choices.why: Right: the import is a code path that writes and deletes nothing, and the TTL is the only net.

choices.text: The import fails because the keys exist
choices.why: The database knows nothing about the cache; the import succeeds.

prompt: In the plain run, how many times did fifty simultaneous requests for one missing key run the count?
hint: The program and pg_stat_statements agree.

prompt: Why did each of the fifty counts take about 1.3 s on average, when a single count took 55 ms?
hint: Four processors.

choices.text: Redis slowed down under fifty connections
choices.why: The time is in the database's own execution, which pg_stat_statements measured.

choices.text: The count took locks that made the others wait in turn
choices.why: A count takes no lock that blocks another count.

choices.text: Fifty scans shared four processors
choices.why: Right: each ran far slower because of the other forty-nine.

choices.text: The first query evicted the table from memory
choices.why: Nothing evicted it; the cost is contention, not cache misses.

prompt: Inside `single_flight`, why does the lock holder look in the cache again before querying?
hint: An earlier version made two queries.

choices.text: To renew the lock's ten-second expiry so it outlives the long query
choices.why: A get does not touch the lock.

choices.text: In case the previous holder stored the value while it waited
choices.why: Right: a released lock lets the next caller in, so it must check the work is still needed.

choices.text: Because Redis requires a read before every write inside a lock
choices.why: It requires nothing of the kind.

choices.text: To count the hit in `seen`
choices.why: `seen` is in dashboard.py, not in stampede.py.

prompt: In `single_flight`, `cache.set(LOCK, 1, nx=True, ex=10)` succeeds for only one caller because `nx` means: set only if the key does ___ exist.
hint: Two letters, one of them N.

prompt: Which of these reduce the stampede on a hot key? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section lists three ways besides single flight.

choices.text: A job that refreshes the key before it expires
choices.why: Right: readers never meet a miss.

choices.text: Serving the old value while one request refreshes it
choices.why: Right: nobody waits, and only one refresh runs.

choices.text: A single-flight lock in Redis
choices.why: Right: the run went from fifty queries to one.

choices.text: A longer `max_connections` on PostgreSQL
choices.why: More connections let even more copies of the query run at once.

choices.text: Restarting Redis to clear old keys
choices.why: A restart empties every key at once: the largest stampede there is.

prompt: What did `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY seller_days` answer before the index existed?
hint: It needs to match old rows with new.

choices.text: It refreshed, but blocked readers
choices.why: It did not refresh at all; it refused.

choices.text: That the view must be dropped and recreated before any refresh
choices.why: A plain refresh works without the index; only the concurrent one refuses.

choices.text: That it needs a unique index with no WHERE clause
choices.why: Right: the error and its hint, and `(seller_id, day)` is that index.

choices.text: That the view is out of date
choices.why: It said nothing about freshness.

prompt: The concurrent refresh took 318 ms and the plain one 113 ms. Why does the lesson still prefer the concurrent one for a dashboard read all day?
hint: What does each one do to readers?

choices.text: Readers keep getting answers during it
choices.why: Right: the plain refresh holds a lock that blocks every read of the view.

choices.text: It recomputes only the rows that changed in the tables
choices.why: Every refresh runs the whole query; it applies only the differences.

choices.text: It refreshes automatically after each write
choices.why: No refresh is automatic; you schedule it.

choices.text: It does not need an index on the view
choices.why: It is the one that needs a unique index.

prompt: A shop's pending-orders count must never be more than five seconds old, and is read three hundred times a second. Which design fits the lesson best?
hint: Freshness bound, and a hot key.

choices.text: A materialized view refreshed once an hour
choices.why: An hour breaks the five-second bound.

choices.text: Cache-aside with a one-day TTL and delete-on-write
choices.why: Every order would delete the key; a lost delete leaves it wrong for a day.

choices.text: No cache, and three hundred counts a second
choices.why: Possible, and exactly the load a cache exists to avoid.

choices.text: A short TTL with single flight
choices.why: Right: the TTL bounds the age, and single flight keeps each expiry to one query.
